title: In new fiction from Rod Moody-Corbett, two Canadian PhD creative writing students find themselves stuck on loan to the armed forces

We no longer await the Canadians, and yet the war—if I can still call it that—proceeds apace. To the east, beyond the airfield and abandoned fitness pavilion with its network of wooded running trails and cryptic gym equipment, comes the pop and scrawl of illumination mortars scurrying across a night sky hazed in graying ash. I can’t speak to the strategic significance of these exercises, to the purpose, whether diversionary or more uniquely incursive, of these bright and painless barrages, but the mortars are truly beautiful to behold. I believe the embered bends trembling from their parachuted flares resemble twisty, slow-moving meteor showers. Star stuff shedding flame.

Caleb doesn’t think so. He submits that once again I am privileging sound over sense and not in a good way; further, my propensity—his word—for abstraction obscures that wanted thisness, by which I understand him to mean, on this night, “reality.”

“I might’ve accepted stellar cinder,” he says. “Molecular cloud. Cosmic outburst.” He peeps his monocular through a slit in our camper’s burlap-frilled window, panning west. The monocular is sludge-brown with a cozy foam eyecup. Caleb ordered it online from an army surplus retailer in Moncton along with the seaweed-green carry pouch, matching belt loop, and lanyard. “Maybe celestial nebulae?”

Before us: bone-white birches, firs, a lattice of matted spruce. Once upon a time, Canadian soldiers deformed from this foliage clothed in shaggy Ghillie suits whose camouflage assumed (or aspired to assume) the timber template of the day. But now, no. Not so much. A Canadian hasn’t graced our lot in weeks.

“You mind with the window?” I ask.

The October air is cool but profuse with wildfire smoke. Already the inside of our trailer smells of smoldered lawn furniture, blackened patios, impassive garden gnomes blistered with melt.

“No can do,” Caleb says. “Carcinogens are par for the territory. You’ll recall the Americans spritzed this coppice with all sorts of chemical defoliants and unregistered herbicides, the likes of which enjoyed far graver exploitation in such provinces as—”

“They’re not coming,” I say. “Not tonight. Not tomorrow night.”

“Quảng Ngãi,” Caleb says. “Gia Lai. Only you can prevent a forest.”

A mortar lofts, and the birches, backlit by a strobing orange glow, adopt a bronchial posture. I’ve compared these trees to lungs, X-rayed lungs, more than twice. Caleb approves of this image in part because it reminds him of a line from a poem by Margaret Atwood. Neither of us can remember the exact line (or the poem or collection from which this line derives), but we frequently rattle off titles as a means of navigating this absence, what Caleb calls our “condition of longing and exile.”

“How to Tell One Country from Another,” I say.

“The Disasters of War: A Sequel.”

“Machine. Gun. Nest.”

“The Loneliness of the Military Historian.”

It bears mentioning that Caleb and I are creative writing students, prospective PhDs, from the University of New Brunswick.

We make $3,500 per operation, receive 10 percent off select nonalcoholic beverages at the Alden Nowlan House, and serve at the pleasure of the Suppositional Insurgency Mentorship Program (SIMP) on behalf of the Canadian Armed Forces. The posting from CAF trickled in through our departmental listserv in March. God knows what prompted Caleb to enlist—the guy’s rolling in funds—but I’m in it for the cash. Notwithstanding that this, our third and most protracted op, looks to be our least remunerative outing yet.

According to our program coordinator, Bella Fermor, our goal, simply stated, is to “assist in the staging and storying of convoluted military simulations engineered to confirm the combat capability of those operational units stationed at 5 CDSB Gagetown in the face of threats foreign and domestic, with particular attention paid to asymmetric advances propagating on the southern border.”

In a word, we roleplay. We cosplay, we LARP.

To date, our credits include a raft of unsavory white boys. Q-pilled incels and transphobic CrossFit enthusiasts. Ball-tanning edgelords with long lusterless beards and diminishing returns on their Twitch streams.

I concede that Caleb presents far more authentically in his homespun boogaloo garb: steel-toe Dakotas, mica-black cargos, and tac vest; camp-collared aloha with its perky toucans and palm fronds and silky, pink-yellow petals of Hawaiian hibiscus; tinted Oakleys and their weird ear stirrups. The tac vest accommodates two fifteen-pound plates (front and back) and is intended for rucking, dipping, and chinning exclusively. danger, the plates read, these plates are not bulletproof. And yet I’m betting they withstand their share of the non-lethal, paraffin-tipped “lipstick” rounds to which our would-be aggressors incline.

Me, I strive for a subtler, somewhat measured rendering. Bella defined our Current Insurgency Status (CIS) as “American, antic.” I feel that my all-weather, black-on-red mackinaw, rusty chinos, 2YT4U hoodie, and mud-spattered Under Armour sneaks verily uphold her designation.

I speak for everyone in our cohort when I say that we’ve all grown a little sick and tired of Caleb’s unceasing accolades and output.

Perhaps Caleb desires to mutate this experience into fiction. Or, failing fiction, participatory journalism. Far be it from me to denigrate the achievements of a fellow writer, but I speak for everyone in our cohort when I say that we’ve all grown a little sick and tired of Caleb’s unceasing accolades and output. Bitbuy Ann Cuthbert Rae Award for Emerging Writers. CBC Poetry Prize. Inaugural Loomcroft Review Chapbook Honorarium for Experimental Fiction. Et cetera. An unabashed self-promoter, back in Fredericton, in his swanky, two-bedroom, quartz-countered riverside condo, under the handle of @theswolenovelette, Caleb uploads topless book content to his TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram channels, entreating his many tens of thousands of admirers to Jell-O-y pec twerks and freeform, pseudo-literary homilies like “27 Short Novels You Can Read in January to Maximize Your Reading Gains” and “Top Three Reasons Why Listening to Within a Budding Grove at 2.5x Speed Still Counts as Reading Proust” and “The Complete Stories of Morley Callaghan: Ranked!”

For the past however many weeks, we’ve been holed up in this wheelless, taupe-paneled mausoleum, subsisting on ramen, tinned tuna, muesli, and tea. The Saint John flooded its banks months ago—worse than ’08, says Caleb, whose people hail from Wakefield Parish—and the ground on which the Canadians lashed our motorhome with braided mooring rope squelches underfoot.

We continue to obtain biweekly provisions, fresh boxers and socks, from the bear-proof bin located in the lamplit glade at the edge of our lot. In vain I have struggled to intercept these deliveries, to converse with someone, anyone, other than Caleb. But our couriers operate under a veil of grating secrecy, presumably at night. What’s more, we sleep well. Camomile—the tea du jour at 5 CDSB Gagetown—is a natural soporific, and I suppose it’s possible that they drug us, lace our bouillon cubes with zolpidem. I wouldn’t put it past them.

Meantime, we’ve kept busy.

Caleb rehearses complex calisthenics—handstands, L-sits, planches—under the shade of our retractable, candy-striped awning while listening to mixtapes of prewar podcasts on his WM-3500SP Walkman. By prewar I refer to a period of blissful intimidation. Tariffs, counter tariffs. Delusions of cultic autocracy. The real war, as distinguished from the unfolding dramedy in which Caleb and I play a bit part, hasn’t happened yet. But it just might: On the morning we deployed to Gagetown, the Globe and Mail reported that an American UAV perusing the icy waters of Merchants Bay at a maximum altitude window of 3.5 klicks spotted the vertical rudder and hull of a surfaced Russian sub sunning itself off the coast of Paallavvik. According to a spokesperson for the Department of National Defense, this was a “concerning development.” As for the WM-3500SP Walkman, go figure. Modern technology is verboten.

The podcasts span a panoply of conspiratorial thinking and fervid gym theory. Caleb regales me with recaps. “One weird trick I learned is you can actually target the long head of your bicep doing curls off a slackline like this,” he’ll say. “Keep your grip firm, supinated. Bring yourself up. Now come back down real slow. See how I got my elbows tucked? You gonna wanna hold that.”

The Canadians preloaded our motorhome with a bro-y bedside stack of arcane readables: Beyond Good and Evil, Demons, Leviathan, Erasmus’s Copia, The Complete Essays of Michel de Montaigne, The Game: Penetrating the Secret Society of Pickup Artists, How to Listen with Intention, an omnibus of The Lord of the Rings.

I read Montaigne. Montaigne on solitude, on sorrow, liars, and idleness. I review—as I did in Fredericton—Fiddlehead submissions, compose expansive rejection letters under increasingly abstruse pseudonyms, and convey these letters to the bear-proof bin, where, as often as not, I find handwritten notes from Miriam, my live-in dog-sitter (Ralph well. Misses daddy.), further Fiddlehead slush, and occasional fan mail:

Dear Toby Jeroboam,

I so appreciate your encouraging words and thoughtful feedback on my short fiction short story submission “Against The Bleachers Of Rome,” and I will certainly begin to try to use “quieter dialogue tags” like you have suggested I do. I didn’t realize that my “britishisms”—like when for instance I spelt yogurt wrong or the colonel (although maybe he’ll be a police captain one day lol) says “rather” and “quite right”—how all of this is distracting and bad. This is useful information to me going forward.

Sincerely yours,

Wayne

Sent from my iPhone

Another mortar pops off, the thirteenth or fourteenth of the night. I’ve lost count. I’d like to diversify the language I use in the service of resurrecting these descriptions, but the mortars do in fact pop, a foamless uncorking, gassy and fast.

The sky brightens, the birches lung, and Caleb says, “Projected Slide of an Unknown Soldier,” to which I say, “Hold up a minute. This sounds different.” Subsequent pop, silence. Or, no, maybe not silence. But a buzzy, low-level humming or moan. The burlap curtains billow, draw taut, and billow again, the stiff copper grommets knocking on their rods. Caleb holsters his monocular and crouches under our kitchen table. “You might think to duck,” he says.

The moan tightens, narrows down to what I’d be tempted to call a “helical hiss,” demonic and whistling, a strident whine. I kick open our oven’s busted broiler drawer and take up a pair of muffin pans, huddle under the table with Caleb, and slant the pans’ smooth, butter-slicked wells over my head. Suffice it to say this is not how I envisioned my fifth year at UNB.

I miss Ralph, my senior retriever, his moist snores, our leashless romps in Killarney Park. By all rights, I should be back at my apartment, my shotgun walk-up off Needham, hunched over the old Singer sewing desk I reskinned into a kind of escritoire or davenport—my laptop, Moleskines, and bitten Blackwings at the ready—honing my craft. I’m ABD, but my D’s a shambles, a collection of discrete short stories. By discrete I mean unlinked. By unlinked I mean brazenly discursive, a hodgepodge of amorphous one-offs. I owe my supervisor pages, but we are a nation on the precipice of war. Concessions of artistic and academic practice can be expected.

A fiery surge of something—impact?—detonates in the lamplit glade, and a framed doily flops off our kitchen cabinet, and its glass matting shatters in the sink. I hear voices, Canadian voices, the bark and drill and probing thug-speak of their rugby brood, nickering in the trees, and then nothing.

Caleb springs to his feet and stumbles into the WC. There follows a grainy rasp of porcelain, splashing. The click of a zippo. A piney waft of smoke.

I lose the pans, clamber up the ladder to our shared sleeping garret, and poke open the skylight to assess the wreckage. Our bearproof bin has been uprooted. Its brown metal hood stands canted in the grass. Soot plumes disperse from within the rubbly blast site, and the bin’s innards wither with blaze. So much for our ramen, our tea, our tins of ecologically dubious tuna. And so much for my incoming Fiddlehead slush. I latch the skylight and slither back down the ladder just as Caleb saunters into the galley brandishing a sopping drybag.

“What’s all this?”

“Free men don’t ask,” Caleb says, a probable allusion, but to what? He parks himself at the table and lowers his Oakleys, the whites of his eyes oystered in Visine. He unfastens the bag and out clatters a short, blocky pistol—pearl grip, teal frame, flush slide—a box of ammo, two extended magazines, and what looks like a really thin beer can swaddled in cloth hockey tape, a suppressor.

“Here,” he says, and glides the box of cartridges across the table. PMC Bronze: 9mm Luger. “Come gimme a hand fixing these clips.”

In the real world, in the world of our erstwhile PhDs, Caleb’s SSHRC-funded dissertation, Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Net Borrower; or, What We Talk About When We Talk About Debt Securities, comprises a book-length erasure of Stephen Harper’s 1991 University of Calgary master’s thesis in economics: The Political Business Cycle and Fiscal Policy in Canada. He performed an excerpt at the Beaverbrook Gallery in June. The reading was not well attended; a cluster of unsuspecting gallerygoers, caught in the crossfire of a literary event, fled before Caleb reached the close of his opening sentence, which I reproduce now without permission, verbatim:

Inappropriate circumstances dampen peacetime themes despite obvious errors in liquid feeding—ruining good marriages, displacing “leakages,” while generating excessive, ideological levels of Winter.

I unseal the box of rounds and study them. Blanks? Dud wads? Caps? On each of the casings someone’s etched messages in an impossibly small hand. “Moratorium on unAmerican as synonymous for American,” reads one. “The motorcade pulled into Trump International Golf Club at 9:21 a.m.,” reads another. “Quit honking. See the ‘Elbows up’ sticker on my Tesla,” “Send. Nude. Pics.”

“Caleb?”

He envelops the threaded (female) end of his suppressor over the obligingly coiled glans (as it were) of his pistol, twists. “I’m listening, what?”

Between the treeline and blast site a triptych of up-armored TAPVs lumbers our way. Maybe they’re establishing a perimeter? A luminous green mist issues from the mounted turrets. Prior to our enlistment, we received a chaperoned tour of the vast Quonset hut in which a number of these vehicles are stabled. I know that the turreted ordinance stations, which feature belt-fed, air-cooled machine guns and automatic grenade launchers, are remote controlled and partly enclosed in mesh netting. “Cope cages,” our guide informed us. “Least that’s what the Ukrainians call ‘em.”

Caleb snatches the box of ammo from me and begins backing rounds into one of the magazines, keeping his thumb poised over the springy black pad at the top of the clip. “See how I’m doing this?” he says. “Like a Pez dispenser. Push and down and glide. Push and down and—”

A shell ruptures within a few meters of our power pedestal, showering our vinyl siding in slime. “Time to vamoose,” Caleb says. He slips the magazine into the pistol and racks the slide. “We need to get to the river.”

“But we’re not supposed to leave the trailer,” I say. “The trailer, as stated in Section 6 of our contract, Disciplines of Prudence and Geography, as a land—”

“Don’t quote scripture at me.”

“—a land whose absolute boundary constitutes—”

“We get to the river, we can nab a dingy or johnboat.”

“But what do we need a dingy for?”

“You want to stick around and find out?”

We stagger from our motor home into a roaring simulacrum of combat. The Canadians assail us with impunity. Bullets plink branches and chip picnic tables. Sparks plume and puddles judder. It is an impressive feat of engineering, if nothing else. The Canadians must’ve fortified this entire encampment with squibs and pneumatic tubing. We cower behind our bumper, the knees of my chinos greasing in the sod. Caleb pulls a neoprene balaclava down over his face, and a white script, runic, fluoresces across his lips. He straps on a pair of padded golf gloves, wags a finger at me, a tuft of bushes, me, the pillowy bushes.

“On three,” he says. “One. Two.”

The three is silent, which disturbs me, but no matter. I follow Caleb—Caleb, who despite the vest, the Oakleys, the steel-toe Dakotas, traverses the slurp and skid of this rumbling scene with elf-like nimbleness. My progress is another story. Neither nimble nor especially elfin, I punch through the lumpy shrubbery, a pie-eyed insurrectionist, heeding knurled roots, rocks, stumps, stinging twigs.

“Pick it up,” Caleb says. “Quit looking at your feet.”

North? South? We execute a veering retreat, hanging lefts, rights, lefts, slighter rights. My cardinals are all out of whack. A gaunt path, towered in goldeny conifers (tamaracks?), emerges on our nine, and we slink through it. I envy Caleb’s balaclava. You’d think the Canadians might’ve provided us with N95s, pleated surgical blues, something. It seems borderline actionable to force us to work under these conditions sans PPE; not that anyone consented to our present defection. I cough and spit. A stitch flourishes on the outskirts of what’s either a kidney, my liver, or my gallbladder. With each suck of air, smoke seeps deeper into my lungs.

“Wait,” I say. “Stop. This is ridiculous, this—”

A drone, what looks like a child’s toy helicopter—purple LEDs festoon a shark-shaped chassis—patters overhead, maintaining a queasy flutter. Caleb squats and raises his pistol.

“Please,” I say. “It’s enough already. The ray gun. Your space phaser.”

“Move,” he says.

I try to move, to initiate what, in a first-person shooter, might amount to an oblique scamper or strafe. But my limbs glitch and my mind snows. Another in a long line of Covid holdovers? Caleb shoves me aside and squeezes off a shot. The suppressor’s report sounds like a thumped bible or a heavy load of laundry dropped on a rug. The drone sheds a propellor, and Caleb slaps the pistol’s jammed slide with his palm. Does that track? Have I underestimated the credibility of his weaponry? A second round incapacitates the drone’s square camera (its dominant POV), and the sleek, purple-finned craft sputters to death in a snarl of tawny dogwood. Well, c’est the guerre, non? By the bib of my hoodie I am yanked to my feet. Caleb dusts me off. Plucks a spiny burdock from my sleeve.

“Get your head into this,” he says.

“My head into what?” I say back. “American. Antic. Those’re our orders. Correct me if I’m wrong but—” coughs, spits “—last I checked, antic Americans don’t run.”

“Your mouth,” says Caleb. “I want you to close it.”

A sigh passes from his balaclava’s nostrils in a twirl of wintry steam.

“Your gun isn’t real,” I say. The cartoonish hues, the fang of tape dangling off the suppressor’s aluminum housing. “None of this.”

Caleb tenses a finger over the trigger and fires. There is light and there is sound. Muzzle flash and spurting turf. It occurs to me that Caleb’s orders in no way mirror my own.

“Satisfied?” he says.

We continue along the trail in silence. Or I do. Caleb speaks and I listen, sort of, as we swerve our way down these slick, mucky thickets, eyeing dry ground. Do the Canadians pursue us? As truants, certifiably AWOL, have we defaulted on our contractual agreements? Are we still getting paid?

Caleb says, “Jack. My mother’s great-uncle Jack was captured in Normandy just after D-Day. Landed on the Calvados coast in Juno with the 9 CIB. Which, that’s whatever, infantry. The details are immaterial. Fell in with a militia regiment from Sherbrooke and headed inland where they fought and lost in Authie. Picture urban firefighting. Torched Shermans. Belfried snipers. Crumbling facades. Hummocks of wood waste and stone. I don’t know. I know Jack narrowly avoided execution at the hands of the Hitlerjugend. 12 SS Panzer Division. Seventeen-, eighteen-year-olds. Imagine. Surrendering soldiers not much older than these kids prostrate before their captors. Bayoneted, shot, bludgeoned. How many thwacks of a rifle butt you think it takes to crush a skull? And the gratuitousness of it. The sport. Magazines emptied into bodies already riddled with holes. Corpses stretched out in the road for tanks to mangle. Shapes so badly flattened and smashed villagers had to scrape them off the cobbles with shovels and spades and whatever else just to bury them. The sound a spade makes dragging across rock. A dense rattle and scratch. The French—you know they named a road after that?”

Our pace, in the absence, as now, of any perceivable threat, has slackened some, which comes as no small relief to me and my ailing airways. I’m trying hard not to think too much about what I can’t see, the fine particulate matter suffusing my pinkly ribbed ductwork, my bloodstream. The moon is high and not full and a wan bloom rinses through the scrub, waxing gibbous. You can hear the river, a swollen current rippling swiftly in the middle distance, ten, maybe twenty metres to our approximate south.

Caleb says, “So Jack was captured in Authie. Captured but managed to escape. Rolled into a ditch en route to Caen. Dropped to the ground and played dead. Probably crawled inside a culvert. And a good thing too. L’Abbaye d’Ardenne’s where the real, the more systematized killing went down. Kurt Meyer. The name means nothing to most people. But Waffen-SS General Kurt Meyer’s the one who likely signed off on the carnage. Tried and convicted by a Canadian court in occupied Germany in 1945. Though the trial itself was an embarrassment, a total gong show. I’ve read the transcripts. Witness interviews. Depositions, sworn affidavits. They commuted Meyer’s execution and later his life sentence. Served just about a decade in all. And you know where he did his time? Go ahead, guess.”

“I don’t care.”

“You gotta guess. No fun for me if you don’t guess.”

“Berlin? Munich?”

“We’re naming German cities now?”

“Leipzig? Bremen. Was it Bremen?”

“Dorchester Penitentiary,” Caleb says. “New Brunswick. Bout an hour, hour or two from where we’re at. Did five years in this very province. 1946. Worked as a librarian. Not a bad gig. Ran the prisoners through their daily aerobics. Taught himself English. Sent letters home to his wife and children. Watch your step.”

Caleb grasps a rotten birch branch and hesitates, gauging his next play. “But get this,” he says, thrusting himself forward, striding across a syrupy divot of deadfall and sludge. “Best part, unbelievable, really, you think about it. When they ferried Meyer across the Atlantic, from London to Halifax, they dressed him up in Canadian fatigues to conceal his identity. Jacket, boots, drab-olive pants with the baggy pleats that frill out at the hip. Here is Meyer, then, wandering the deck of the RMS Aquitania, an unrepentant mass murderer. Tricked out in Canadian trousers, not a shackle in sight. Playing cards with the ship’s officers, bidding hale hellos to war brides and tykes. He sits at a window, smoking. Takes the air. Performs chin-ups off a lifeboat’s cast-iron davit. Children watch him, fascinated. He reads Uncle Tom’s Cabin. A favorite of the Führer’s. I shit you not. Onkel Toms Hütte. A Hitler’s pick. Sups on boiled haddock, hardtack, bisque.”

“There’s a point to this story,” I say. “An upshot?”

“Right. So Jack, after the war, returns to New Brunswick. Moves back in with the folks. Takes a job as a correctional officer at the penitentiary in Dorchester. Working nights.”

“This isn’t a true story?”

“Yes and no. But of course not. I’m embellishing everything. By 1951 Meyer is shipped off to Germany. Werl Prison. And in 1954 he is set free. Receives a hero’s welcome. These are the facts. Dons his Nazi medals and writes his memoir, Grenadiers. Lobbies for leniencies on behalf of Waffen-SS vets. But he is a sick man. Kidney and heart disease. Chronic arthritis keeps him in orthopedics and requires that he walk with a cane. Dies on his fifty-first birthday. And in Hagen thousands of mourners attend his funeral. This is Meyer’s story. The facts, as I say. But it is not my story.”

“Jack.”

“Jack exacts his revenge on Meyer. Consider this my revisionist history. Jack gains the general’s confidence over the course of many conversations. They talk politics, communism, family, art. They discover a shared passion for fitness and amphibious battle strategies. Jack assists him with his English. Brings him books. Maybe that H. G. Wells story that forecast the advent of tanks. Can’t remember the title. Anyway. They’re friends. But all the while Jack’s been poisoning him, see. I want to say he mixes strychnine pills into his soup. But I haven’t researched the means, the plausible availabilities. And, of course, there is something of Poe in this. Something of—”

How like a Canadian to pit the ribs of this vessel with surreptitious cavities and loosened rivets.

Our path has petered out on a sheer gravel bank pronged with loose briars and roots. Scrolls of barbed wire entanglements girdle the ridge; the river below is a tarry sluice. Caleb stuffs his pistol into the crotch of his cargos and plunges down the bank, arms pumping. Not me. I ride out the knoll like a trepid tobogganer. Which is to say at my leisure. Ass-wise, heeling dirt.

Caleb switches on his monocular’s night vision and hands me a tactical flashlight. The noise is extraordinary. The rush of waves, muscled and roaring, the churning surf. There are bird prints and blurry wing streaks stitched in the sand and nested all up inside some grayly swaying reeds are bloated pop bottles and flasks, a black jug of high-mileage motor oil, glistening chip bags, a diaper, a phone cord, cords of white nylon test.

“Over here,” Caleb says. “Hurry up.”

A canoe, half-hooded in spruce fronds and notably corroded with rust, juts ashore, its long riveted keel angled up. We flip the boat over and march it into the river.

“No paddles,” I say.

“Don’t matter. Wind’s on our side. Current too. Obviously. We lay low, I’m thinking we make the Nashwaak by morning.”

“Then what?”

“Then nothing. I look forward to a shower, a shave, moisture-wicking gymwear.”

I enter the canoe from the rear and scramble into the bow while Caleb braces the gunnels. Immediately I am chastised for sitting. “Your center of gravity,” Caleb says. “Reconsider it.” He waits until I am kneeling before nudging us away from the beach and hopping aboard; and, for a moment, as the current sweeps us along its spuming chute, a nautical tranquility overwhelms me.

“Maybe I’ll write about this,” I say, running a thumb over the gunnels, strumming the faintly chipped crimp.

“You should,” Caleb says. He has removed one of the fifteen-pound plates from his tac vest and appears to be using it as a rudder. “That’s a great idea. Though I should tell you I’ve had a thing commissioned for months.”

“You’re writing a piece?”

“I am, yeah. But you should too. I’d love to read it. What’s that one story at the airport with the dead wife or the dead man who pretends his wife is dead or—”

“The man’s a widower,” I say. “He pretends his wife is still alive.”

“Right,” Caleb says. “I liked that one.”

A shawl of smoke skates across the water like a vulture’s ragged wing. We are drifting too much into the middle of things and picking up speed. A wave creeps over my knees and our nose spears into a burl of hapless rapids, pitching us forward and wrenching us around on our side.

“Damn,” Caleb says. “We sprung a leak.”

How like a Canadian to pit the ribs of this vessel with surreptitious cavities and loosened rivets. We take on water and sink. Caleb loses the plate and howls wisdom at me—“Form a sealed cup with your palms and bail, bail!”—but I jump ship and he follows. The current swings the canoe down a bubbling trough—gone. I manage to keep my head above water, jolting my arms and legs, a cheerless dogpaddle, but Caleb’s vest is a problem. “Help!” he screams. “Help!”

A wide metal hook with cushioned tines prizes me about the waist and rakes me ashore; a second hook nets Caleb. I close my eyes and imagine myself a member of Jack’s descended world, a body bent on one ambition, a possum, a frog, a common swift, breathing and dead.

The Canadians have rescued us. The Canadians have captured us. I miss Ralph.
